body:
[11.4.2](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x20-V11-Cryptography.md#v114-hashing-and-hash-based-functions) should be:
Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, **key derivation function** with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks **sufficiently** challenging **for the required level of security**.

Reasoning
"hashing algorithm" is a misleading term in context of storing passwords. The correct term is "key derivation function" which is already used in the description of [11.4](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x20-V11-Cryptography.md#v114-hashing-and-hash-based-functions).

"**more** challenging" is imprecise. The required level of security for an application is the relevant factor.

comments.body:
I 100% support this change. bcrypt, scrypt, pbkdf2 and Argon2id are all technically password hashing algorithms **and** KDF's. I think both of your changes add a lot of clarity.

"More challenging" can lead to a DOS vector if you take the config settings too far.

Hi-5 🙌🏽

For future reference, the current wording is:

> Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, **hashing algorithm** with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks more challenging.

> "hashing algorithm" is a misleading term in context of storing passwords. The correct term is "key derivation function" which is already used in the description of [11.4](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x20-V11-Cryptography.md#v114-hashing-and-hash-based-functions).

It is really misleading? "password hashing" is widely used and is understood by everyone. I feel that "password hash" be included in the requirement somehow for clarity.

Some references:

* Argon 2 (RFC 9106) is titled "Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for **Password Hashing** and Proof-of-Work Applications"
* scrypt (RFC 7914) is titled "The scrypt **Password-Based Key Derivation Function**"

The title of Argon 2 RFC is talking about "Password Hashing" and goes further saying:

> This document corresponds to version 1.3 of the Argon2 **hash function**
>
> […]
>
> Argon2i uses data-independent memory access, which is preferred for **password hashing** and password-based key derivation.

So hashing typically refers to a message integrity code function like md5/sha.

I think the term "password hashing function" or KDF is much clearer than just hashing.

One of the most common mistakes devs used to make when building AuthN functionality is to use a message integrity code for password storage.

How about just a small change:

_Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, password hashing algorithm with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks more challenging._

> One of the most common mistakes devs used to make when building AuthN functionality is to use a message integrity code for password storage.

Agreed. We must not mislead the user towards this path.

> Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, password hashing algorithm with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks more challenging.

LGTM.

Nitpick: Currently the appendix subsection title is "Hash Functions for Password Storage". Should we use the same wording in this requirement and in the appendix?

* Should the appendix section be changed into "Password hashing algorithm"?
* Should we use "Password hashing functions" in both?
* Is it OK as it is?

> > Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, password hashing algorithm with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks more challenging.
> 
> LGTM.
> 
> Nitpick: Currently the appendix subsection title is "Hash Functions for Password Storage". Should we use the same wording in this requirement and in the appendix?
> 
> * Should the appendix section be changed into "Password hashing algorithm"?
> * Should we use "Password hashing functions" in both?
> * Is it OK as it is?

I absolutely think this is a good direction to get away from the term "hashing" in this content. I would change the appendix.

If you want to get REALLY pedantic, PBKDF2 is technically a KDF and not a password hashing algorithm.

So I think "password hashing" is good enough.

But "password hashing or key derivation functions" is even better.

But this is - admittedly - super super pedantic. :)

So maybe even:

_11.4.2 Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, password hashing algorithm or key derivation function, with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security._

I think this is the most clear and the most technically accurate.

What do you think @ingo-rauner and @randomstuff ?

*If* KDF is really the better more accurate wording for this, you could even be more explicit:

> 11.4.2 Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (colloquially called “password hashing function”), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.

In your proposed wording, it is somewhat ambiguous whether password hashing algorithm and key derivation function are the same thing or two possible options for achieving the same goal (?).

> _If_ KDF is really the better more accurate wording for this, you could even be more explicit:
> 
> > 11.4.2 Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (colloquially called “password hashing function”), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
> 
> In your proposed wording, it is somewhat ambiguous whether password hashing algorithm and key derivation function are the same thing or two possible options for achieving the same goal (?).

I like this direction. The only problem is, not all KDF's are password hashing functions. Like HKDF (HMAC‑based Key Derivation Function, RFC 5869) is not meant for password storage.

So the real answer is:

"an approved password hashing function or some approved KDF's that can also be used for password hashing"

And this is complex and pedantic, sorry for this.
Can someone open a PR which is not too complex but handles the subtleties? @jmanico @ingo-rauner @randomstuff
Great pull request, @jmanico . Thank you @randomstuff and @jmanico for your comments.
